tldr: A whole-body control framework that coordinates quadrupedal base motion and arm manipulation purely from short-horizon end-effector trajectories, achieving zero-shot generalization across four arm morphology families and executing tasks far beyond the arm's fixed-base reach.
hero_caption: Overview of PolyMorphWBC. Taking short-horizon end-effector (EE) preview trajectories as input, a shared hierarchical controller generates coordinated arm-base motions. It (a) supports diverse arm morphologies with different fixed-base reaches and (b) autonomously previews and moves the base to track trajectories extending well beyond the initial reach.
overview:
Quadrupedal mobile manipulators—quadrupeds equipped with a robotic arm—are compelling platforms combining high leg traversability with arm dexterity. A popular design paradigm takes short-horizon end-effector (EE) trajectories from modern Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and executes them via low-level whole-body control (WBC). However, when the EE travels beyond the arm's reach, the controller must anticipate when and how the base should move. Worse yet, changing the arm's geometry or mass distribution dramatically shifts not only its reachable workspace but also the reaction forces (disturbances) exerted on the base. Traditional controllers therefore had to be re-engineered from scratch for each specific arm.

To address this, the authors introduce PolyMorphWBC, a hierarchical whole-body controller driven solely by task-level EE trajectories that generalizes across four distinct arm families. At its core is a three-layer architecture: a whole-body coordinator that determines base velocity and posture from previewed EE targets, an arm-specific IK solver that accurately tracks the instantaneous target, and a frozen locomotion backend resilient to dynamic disturbances. By pairing a supervised "morphology conditioning" embedding pre-trained on arm URDF kinematics and dynamics with real-time "online residual-wrench feedback," PolyMorphWBC seamlessly adapts to unseen arm morphologies.

In simulation, PolyMorphWBC achieved a 93.95% completion rate on unseen arm morphologies and trajectories, cutting position error by ~70% and orientation error by over 90% compared to the prior SOTA (UMI-on-Legs). On physical hardware combining a Unitree Go2 with an ARX5 arm, the system successfully performed extended-reach pick-and-place tasks using only EE trajectories from a VLA model ($\pi_0$), without requiring explicit base navigation commands.
contributions: Proposed a hierarchical whole-body control architecture that takes only short-horizon EE preview trajectories and generates coordinated motions extending well beyond the initial reach without explicit base navigation commands.
Integrated URDF-derived static morphology conditioning with online residual-wrench feedback, allowing a single trained controller to be reused across four distinct arm families.

Reduced EE position error by 69–72% and orientation error by 91–97% compared to UMI-on-Legs in MuJoCo, and demonstrated language-conditioned extended-reach pick-and-place on a physical Go2–ARX5 system using the $\pi_0$ VLA model.

sections.heading: Moving Legs and Arms from End-Effector Trajectories Alone—and Why Swapping the Arm Breaks It
sections.summary: While end-effector trajectories provide a clean interface for high-level policies like VLAs, whole-body workspace extension depends heavily on arm morphology. PolyMorphWBC integrates trajectory preview with arm morphology information to enable arm-agnostic, extended-reach whole-body control.
sections.details:
A major advantage of quadrupedal mobile manipulators is that the legs can transport the base to reach targets far beyond the arm's standalone workspace. Capitalizing on this flexibility, recent pipelines use short-horizon end-effector (EE) trajectories predicted by Diffusion Policies or Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models as task commands, relying on a low-level whole-body controller (WBC) to distribute motion between legs and arms. The beauty of this EE trajectory interface is that high-level task planners do not have to worry about low-level base coordination.

However, making this work introduces two tightly coupled challenges:
- First, when the EE moves beyond the arm's fixed-base reach, the controller must anticipate this and move or rotate the base in advance. If base movement lags, the arm falls short; if the base moves too aggressively, EE tracking accuracy and robot balance deteriorate.
- Second, this coordination heavily depends on arm "morphology." Changing link lengths or joint configurations completely alters the workspace geometry, requiring different base motions for the exact same EE trajectory. Varying mass distributions also drastically alter the dynamic disturbance wrench transmitted to the base.

Prior work has almost exclusively trained policies specialized for a single arm. In contrast, PolyMorphWBC leverages previewed EE trajectories for base decision-making and couples URDF-derived morphology features with online dynamic feedback, delivering a reusable whole-body controller across a diverse spectrum of arm morphologies.

A shared hierarchical controller consumes a 1-second preview of the EE trajectory to autonomously generate coordinated arm-base motions tailored to the arm morphology. It smoothly tracks trajectories (b) extending far beyond the fixed-base reach (a) by coordinating the mobile base.

sections.heading: At the Crossroads of Whole-Body Control, Morphology Generalization, and Visuomotor Policies
sections.summary: Traditional whole-body control relied heavily on fixed arm setups using mathematical optimization or reinforcement learning. This work bridges robot morphology generalization and recent visuomotor policies (e.g., VLAs) to create an arm-swappable EE trajectory tracking controller.
sections.details:
### Trends in Whole-Body Control (WBC)
Whole-body control for quadrupedal manipulators spans classical model predictive control (MPC) and hierarchical optimization (such as ALMA), as well as reinforcement learning (RL) approaches trained in simulation (DeepWBC, VBC, RoboDuet, etc.). More recently, learning-based tracking frameworks driven by EE trajectories like UMI-on-Legs have emerged. However, these methods typically assume a single fixed arm morphology and focus on workspaces close to the base, offering limited support for swapping arms or handling long-range extended reach.

### Cross-Morphology Control Across Robots
Techniques for handling dynamic variations include online latent variable estimation (e.g., RMA), disturbance wrench-aware locomotion, and cross-morphology policies trained across randomized quadrupeds (GenLoco, LocoFormer). This paper keeps the base quadruped platform (Unitree Go2) fixed while substantially varying the kinematic and inertial parameters of the mounted 6-DoF arm. It achieves novelty by combining an explicit static morphology representation, arm-specific IK, and online interaction feedback.

### Visuomotor Policies and Task Interfaces
Recent large-scale robot foundation models like ACT, Diffusion Policy, OpenVLA, and $\pi_0$ standardly output short-term action chunks (sequences of EE poses). PolyMorphWBC is purposefully designed to serve as an execution foundation that directly consumes these task-level EE trajectories.

sections.heading: How PolyMorphWBC Works: The Triad of Preview, Morphology Embedding, and Residual Wrench
sections.summary: The method comprises three layers: a whole-body coordinator, an arm-specific IK solver, and a locomotion backend. Combining pre-trained URDF morphology representations with real-time residual-wrench feedback enables seamless whole-body coordination across unseen arms.
sections.details:
### III-A System Overview
The control interface accepts only short-horizon EE trajectories. Specifically, it feeds a preview $\mathbf{p}_t$ of $K=7$ future target poses (relative translation and continuous 6D rotation, totaling 9 dimensions) spanning up to 1 second ahead in the base frame. The system coordinates motion across three hierarchical layers:
- **Whole-Body Coordinator ($\pi_W$)**: Runs at 10 Hz. Conditioned on the preview trajectory $\mathbf{p}_t$, robot state, and morphology embedding $\mathbf{z}^W_m$, it outputs base planar velocity targets ($v_x, v_y, \omega_z$) along with base pitch and height targets ($\theta_B, h_B$).
- **Arm-Specific IK Solver ($\mathrm{IK}_m$)**: Runs at 50 Hz. It strictly solves the instantaneous EE target using the arm's specific kinematic model via Damped Least Squares (DLS) to produce arm joint targets $\mathbf{q}^a_t$.
- **Locomotion Backend ($\pi_B$)**: Runs at 50 Hz. It tracks the base commands produced by the coordinator and outputs leg joint torques/positions $\mathbf{a}^\ell_t$.

### III-B Arm Morphology Representation and Pre-training
The study targets four representative 6-DoF arm families used in industry and research: ARX X5, PiPER, Compact xArm6, and Compact MICO. Based on family templates, link lengths and mass properties are procedurally randomized to generate diverse arm variants. Their URDF descriptors $\boldsymbol{\theta}_m$ are passed through a morphology encoder $E_\phi$ pre-trained on two supervised tasks:
- **Kinematics Decoder**: Predicts EE positions and related metrics from joint configurations.
- **Dynamics Decoder**: Predicts the base reaction wrench from joint positions, velocities, and accelerations.
Once trained, the encoder is frozen and provides morphology embeddings to downstream policies.

### III-C Residual-Wrench-Conditioned Locomotion Backend
Static URDF parameters cannot fully capture dynamic disturbances and tracking lags caused by rapid arm motions. Therefore, the online "residual wrench" (disturbance force and torque) $\bar{\mathbf{w}}^a_{B,t}$ exerted by the arm links on the base is computed in real time. This wrench, along with an $N_h=5$ step response history $\mathbf{H}_t$, is supplied to the locomotion backend. Using PPO in IsaacLab, a robust locomotion policy is trained to resist aggressive arm movements and unknown reaction loads without tipping over.

### III-D Whole-Body Coordinator Training
Finally, with the morphology encoder and locomotion backend frozen, the whole-body coordinator $\pi_W$ is trained using PPO. The training set includes structured trajectories both within the fixed-base reach and across "extended-reach" zones. The reward function incentivizes EE position and orientation tracking accuracy, base-to-EE heading alignment, and minimal unnecessary base motion, while penalizing joint limits and collisions to elicit smooth preview-based navigation.

(b) Pre-training the morphology encoder on kinematics and dynamics from URDF descriptors. (c) Locomotion backend PPO training under arm disturbances via offline IK. (d) Whole-body coordinator RL training with the frozen locomotion backend.

sections.heading: Experimental Results: Reaching Beyond Workspace Limits in Simulation and on Real Hardware
sections.summary: PolyMorphWBC achieved a 93.95% completion rate on unseen arms and extended trajectories, reducing orientation error by over 90% compared to UMI-on-Legs. On a physical Go2–ARX5 robot, it executed extended-reach pick-and-place guided solely by EE trajectories from $\pi_0$.
sections.details:
### IV-A Experimental Setup
The base platform was a Unitree Go2. For the arms, 1,024 procedurally generated models were used for training and 128 held-out variants for evaluation across the four families, alongside four real-world anchor models (ARX X5, PiPER, Compact xArm6, and Compact MICO). As a baseline, the authors compared zero-shot tracking performance against UMI-on-Legs in MuJoCo. Hardware experiments mounted an ARX X5 on a Go2 for teleoperation and autonomous pick-and-place powered by the $\pi_0$ VLA model.

### IV-B Simulation Evaluation
- **Generalization to Unseen Arms and Trajectories**: Across all held-out evaluation sets, PolyMorphWBC achieved a 93.95% completion rate, with an average position error of 2.30 cm and an orientation error of 4.81°. On extended trajectories reaching more than 1.0 m forward ($x > 1$ m), it maintained a 94.83% completion rate (1.94 cm position error); for rear trajectories ($x < 0$), it reached 91.56% (2.41 cm position error).
- **Transfer to Anchor Arms**: On the real-world anchor models excluded from training, it achieved a 99.30% completion rate on the ARX X5 (1.57 cm error) and 99.27% on the xArm6 (1.93 cm error), highlighting strong generalization.
- **Comparison with UMI-on-Legs (MuJoCo)**: Across four circular and square trajectories, UMI-on-Legs exhibited position errors of 4.77–7.31 cm and large orientation errors of 22.72°–76.57°. PolyMorphWBC achieved position errors of 1.38–2.04 cm (a 69–72% reduction) and orientation errors of 2.01°–2.38° (a 91–97% reduction). While UMI-on-Legs reacts only after the arm nears its limits—causing orientation tracking to collapse—PolyMorphWBC previewed future targets and preserved steady orientation.

### IV-C Ablation Studies
Removing morphology conditioning caused completion rates to plunge by 2.59 to 9.90 percentage points on geometrically distinct arm families (Compact xArm6 and Compact MICO). This confirms that explicit morphology information is vital for handling diverse arm mechanisms within a unified policy.

### IV-D Real-Robot Experiments
On the physical Go2–ARX5 setup, the controller was driven by teleoperated EE poses and image-based EE predictions from $\pi_0$. In neither case were explicit base commands supplied. Nevertheless, the quadruped autonomously walked forward and adjusted its base posture in coordination with the EE trajectory, successfully picking and placing objects positioned far outside the arm's standalone reach.

captions.F3: Trajectory tracking comparisons on Go2–ARX5 in MuJoCo. Target trajectory is shown in dashed black, PolyMorphWBC in blue, and UMI-on-Legs in orange. Across all four trajectories (a–d), PolyMorphWBC precisely tracks the target path and EE orientation (arrows).
captions.F4: Real-world demonstrations on the Go2–ARX5 platform. (a) Teleoperation via end-effector inputs (red arrows denote EE commands, red curves show autonomously generated base paths). (b) Language-conditioned extended-reach pick-and-place using $\pi_0$. Both achieve whole-body coordination without explicit base navigation commands.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Future Outlook
sections.summary: PolyMorphWBC demonstrates that trajectory preview and morphology adaptation can achieve reach-extended whole-body control across varied arm types. Future steps include generalizing across different quadruped bases and tackling contact-rich manipulation.
sections.details:
This paper introduced PolyMorphWBC, a hierarchical whole-body controller for quadrupedal mobile manipulators that uses short-horizon end-effector (EE) trajectories as its sole motion interface while extending reachable workspaces across diverse arm morphologies.

By leveraging trajectory previews to anticipate when to move the base, and combining URDF morphology conditioning, arm-specific IK, and real-time residual wrench feedback, a single pre-trained policy generalizes zero-shot across multiple arm families. Simulation and real-world experiments confirm its tracking precision and seamless integration with VLA models.

Current limitations include relying on known arm URDF parameters, an assumption of smooth and relatively low-speed EE trajectories, and restriction to the Unitree Go2 base. The authors highlight porting the framework to alternative quadruped bases and extending it to contact-rich manipulation tasks as promising directions for future work.

takeaways: Supplying a preview of future EE trajectories enables reinforcement learning to autonomously discover optimal base movement timing for extended-reach tasks without explicit base commands.
Fusing pre-trained URDF morphology embeddings (kinematics/dynamics) with online residual-wrench feedback allows a single controller to generalize across four diverse 6-DoF arm families.

A hierarchical design that directly consumes action chunks from VLA models (e.g., $\pi_0$) and turns them into coordinated base motions bridges high-level task learning and low-level whole-body control seamlessly.
limitations: The mobile base is fixed to the Unitree Go2; it has not been validated across differing quadruped platform morphologies (e.g., larger quadrupeds or bipeds).
The controller assumes relatively smooth, low-speed EE trajectories, leaving performance under aggressive acrobatic maneuvers or sudden large disturbances unverified.
Accurate arm URDF models are required ahead of time; unmodeled joint friction or heavy backlash could degrade performance.
Evaluation centered primarily on free-space trajectory tracking; handling contact-rich tasks like opening heavy doors remains an open challenge.
